Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 27-year-old Sinhalese from the capital of my home country. After spending two years in London, U.K., I returned home in 2006 and became involved in politics. I worked for a political party during the municipal elections under the guidance of a family friend, who is a well-known politician. I was an active member and served as a special assistant to this politician. During the election campaign, the Election Commission rejected our party’s candidature because one candidate was not 18 years old by the nomination deadline. As a result, our party allied with another party, which eventually won the municipal elections.

During and after the elections, I received death threats from the opposition party and, in particular, from the supporters of a powerful politician. The situation escalated in mid-2006 when I witnessed the mayor being bribed by a criminal working for the opposition. The criminal tried to convince the mayor to break our party’s alliance and form a new one with the opposition. I ran away and immediately informed my political mentor about what I had seen. The two men involved in the bribery noticed my presence and, according to what I was told, wanted to eliminate me. I was warned that if they ever saw me again, they would kill me.

After this, I went into hiding. Thugs associated with the powerful politician came to my home and beat up my uncle and other family members while searching for me. Fearing for my life, I left my home country on October 5th, 2006, and arrived in Toronto the same day. I claimed refugee status 13 days later.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am a 27-year-old woman from my home country. I had a romantic relationship with the daughter of my employer. When my employer discovered our relationship, my employer made threats against me. On one occasion, while I was riding a motorcycle, I was hit by a car. The driver of the car was acting on the instructions of my former employer. After this incident, I continued to receive threatening phone calls and was unsafe.

Because of the ongoing threats, I moved to another area within my country, hoping that I would be safe there. The threats and phone calls continued even after I relocated. My former employer has significant contacts within the government and the police force, which means they could find me no matter where I moved in my country. The authorities would not provide me with any assistance or protection because of my former employer’s influence.

Fearing for my safety and unable to find protection in my country, I left. In 2006, I traveled to Canada. On January 16, 2007, I asked for protection in Canada because I was afraid to return to my home country due to the threats and harm I experienced as a result of my relationship and my former employer’s actions.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a citizen of my home country and I am unable to return there because I fear my former common-law husband, whom I began living with in 1994. I left him because he physically abused me. During the time I lived with him, he beat me regularly. In 1996, I was kicked in the stomach and suffered a miscarriage as a result of the violence. After leaving him, I married my current husband in 1997.

In 1998, my former partner beat my husband, accusing him of stealing his wife, and threatened to kill both of us. Because of these threats and the ongoing danger, my husband and I left for the United Kingdom in 1998, where we made a claim for asylum based on my husband's political opinion due to his association with the opposition party. That claim was rejected in 2001. We then moved to the United States in 2002 and made another asylum claim, also based on my husband's political opinion, but this claim was rejected in 2008.

My two children were born in the United Kingdom. We remained in the United States until 2009, when my husband was deported to my home country. After his deportation, in 2009, my former partner tried to kill my husband in my home country. Fearing for our safety, I traveled to Canada with my two children and made a refugee protection claim based on my membership in a particular social group: an abused woman at the hands of my ex-boyfriend. If I return to my home country, my former partner will try to harm or kill me because he is angry that I left him and remarried. I have not seen him since 1997, but the threats and violence have continued to affect my life and safety.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a member of the Roma minority in my home country. Throughout my life, I have faced discrimination, harassment, and violence because of my ethnicity. This discrimination has affected every aspect of my life, including employment, education, housing, and my interactions with the general public.

Between 2002 and 2011, I and members of my family were physically attacked and assaulted on several occasions by unidentified assailants. These attacks were carried out by people motivated by racism, including police officers, members of organizations or groups, school officials, employers, neighbours, and store owners. The violence and harassment were not isolated incidents but part of a pattern of hostility directed at us because we are Roma.

In addition to physical assaults, we experienced ongoing discrimination in accessing health care and education. My children and I were treated unfairly by school officials, and we were often denied opportunities that were available to others. In the health care system, we faced obstacles and were not treated with the same respect or urgency as others. Discrimination was also present in the workplace, where I was denied jobs or treated poorly by employers because of my ethnicity. Our neighbours and people in our community would harass us, making it clear that we were not welcome.

Despite these challenges, I tried to seek help from the authorities, but the police and other officials either did not take our complaints seriously or were themselves involved in the discrimination. I did not feel that the state would protect us or that there was any way for us to live safely and with dignity in my home country. Fearing for our safety and the future of my family, we left our home country and arrived in Canada in 2011. We made a claim for refugee protection on the same day, hoping to find safety and a chance to live free from persecution.

My wife, the mother of my two daughters, died in Saudi Arabia in 2008. I am afraid to return to my home country because of the risk of forced conscription, punishment for evading military service, my political opinions, and my conversion to Christianity.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. Together with my husband, I owned and operated a business in my home country since 1995. In 2006, we borrowed 1.7 million pesos from private lenders at an interest rate of 5% per month, compounded. For the first year, we managed to pay the interest and a small portion of the principal. After that year, we could no longer keep up with the payments. In 2007, the lenders demanded that we either pay the outstanding amount or surrender our home as payment for the interest due. Knowing that we would never be able to repay the loan, we decided to abandon our house to the lenders.

In 2008, at the invitation of a relative, my husband and I flew to Canada. We entered on a six-month visitor’s visa. When our visa expired, we applied for an extension, but it was refused. We remained in Canada without status for another three and a half years before applying to stay on humanitarian grounds. When that application was denied, we claimed refugee protection.

We fear returning to our home country because the lenders could sue us for the unpaid debt. If we lost the lawsuit, we would face jail time under harsh conditions. There are no bankruptcy laws in my home country that would protect us from imprisonment for this kind of debt. The prospect of being imprisoned in such conditions is what forced us to leave and seek protection elsewhere.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a 34-year-old man from my home country. I worked as a seaman starting in 1993. My last assignment was on a motor vessel that arrived in North Vancouver in 2005. At that time, I decided to leave the ship and remain in Canada. I left the ship because I wanted to seek better wages and working conditions for seamen, and I hoped to find an organization that could help fight for the rights of seamen from my country. However, I was afraid to make a complaint, even if I found such an organization.

Another reason I left was because, in 1992, I tried to join the army in my home country. Although I passed all the requirements, I was ultimately rejected. This was because I belong to a minority ethnic group. This experience showed me that I would always face discrimination and limited opportunities in my home country.

After I left the ship, the shipping company contacted my parents several times, telling them that they had suffered a financial penalty because of my actions. They demanded my contact information in Canada and threatened my family, seeking repayment of a large sum of money in U.S. dollars. My father received the first phone call from the company in 2005. The police, or Public Security Bureau, also went to my father's house and left a summons for me. Since then, the neighborhood community patrol has continued to visit my family every one to one and a half months, asking questions about me.

I am afraid that if I return to my home country, I will be punished for leaving the ship without permission. There is evidence that people in my situation are harshly dealt with, including imprisonment and harsh treatment. Some families of ship jumpers have had their houses and possessions confiscated. Although this has not happened to my family yet, the authorities continue to pressure them. I have no way to repay the penalty demanded by the shipping company. I fear that if I return, I will face persecution and my family will continue to be threatened.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. In 2006, I borrowed MXN$40,000 from a man in my home country. I promised to pay the money back later that year. When the time came to repay the loan, I was only able to give him MXN$10,000 because I did not have the full amount. He had me sign an IOU, but it did not state the balance of the principal debt. When I refused to pay this amount, he became very aggressive toward me. I tried to come to an agreement with him, but he continued to threaten me.

I began to fear for my life because of his threats. My spouse and I moved to several different locations within my home country, but each time, we were tracked down. The threats continued, and I felt that we were not safe anywhere. At one point, I was attacked at gunpoint by this man. He fired shots into the air during the attack, which made me fear that he would kill me. My spouse was also assaulted while I was away.

I went to the Public Prosecutor’s office to file a complaint after receiving death threats, but my complaint was not accepted because I did not have any evidence. After the attack at gunpoint, I did not file another complaint because I believed that the authorities would not assist me unless I had overwhelming evidence. I did not seek help from other federal authorities or human rights organizations because I did not think they would help either.

Fearing for our safety, I left my country on a specific date in 2008 and arrived in Montréal, Canada, the same day. I claimed refugee protection one month later in Montréal. Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a person of Korean ancestry from my home country. As a member of the Korean Chinese community, I have experienced prejudice and unfair treatment throughout my life. In 1995, I attended a specialized school to improve my situation and eventually secured my first job in 2002. I worked in difficult and sometimes dangerous conditions from 2002 until I arrived in Canada in February 2006. The work was hard, and the pay was not what had been promised. I, along with others, was physically abused. Because I am Korean Chinese, I was subjected to even worse treatment than my non-Korean colleagues.

In 2006, I was struck on the side of my head by a supervisor, which injured my ear. When the ship arrived in Vancouver, I was allowed to see a doctor. After that, I did not return to the ship. Instead, I went to Chinatown and received help to make a claim for refugee protection.

I am owed outstanding pay from my work, and I have made a complaint through an international federation. The company that operated the ship, as well as the Chinese state-owned company that supplied me, responded by claiming that I owe them money. My family in my home country has been visited by representatives of these companies and by the Public Security Bureau. I am being sued for 210,000 renminbi, a sum I will never be able to pay. Since I am in Canada, I cannot defend myself in court, and I expect a default judgment will be entered against me. As a result, I will be jailed if I return to my home country. My situation is made worse because of my Korean ancestry, as Korean Chinese workers are treated more harshly than others. My fear is based on my experiences of discrimination, the abuse I suffered at work, and the legal actions being taken against me.

After this, I went to the capital and stayed with an agent hired by my brother. I left my home country in 2010.

Throughout these events, I was targeted because of my ethnicity and perceived political associations. I fear that if I return, I will face further harm from the authorities and paramilitary groups, who have already detained, beaten, and extorted money from me, and who continue to threaten people like me.

My family and I experienced many difficulties as members of a minority group in that area. We suffered from the actions of both the national army and armed groups, as well as paramilitary groups that collaborated with the authorities. In 2006, my brother fled to another country after the national army accused him of supporting an armed opposition group.

In 2007, I was detained by the national army for seven days at a military camp on suspicion of supporting the opposition group. During my detention, I was interrogated, threatened, and beaten. I was released only after my wife paid a bribe of 50,000 rupees. After the defeat of the opposition group in May 2009, I was detained again by the national army at another camp, along with others. Paramilitary men assisted the army during this time. A neighbor, who was suspected of supporting the opposition group, was killed. I was questioned, beaten, and tortured, and then released after ten days when my wife paid two of the five lakhs demanded by the army.

Later in 2009, paramilitary men came to my house to extort five lakhs from me. They said this time the money was for them and told me to ask my brother abroad for help. They threatened to report me to the army as a supporter of the opposition group if I did not pay. I gave them one lakh and promised to pay the rest in six months. After this, I went to the capital and stayed with an agent hired by my brother. I left my home country in 2010.

Throughout these events, I was targeted because of my ethnicity and perceived political associations. I fear that if I return, I will face further harm from the authorities and paramilitary groups, who have already detained, beaten, and extorted money from me, and who continue to threaten people like me.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I was raised in my home country in a troubled household. My father was an alcoholic and used marijuana, and he was abusive towards me and my family. I experienced numerous incidents of abuse from him throughout my childhood. Because of the situation at home, I left my country and arrived in Canada in December 1999. After he withdrew his sponsorship application, I learned about it through a letter from immigration authorities dated December 27, 2006.

I fear returning to my home country because my father will kill me if I go back. I have no means to support myself there. My mother has been living in another country, Trinidad and Tobago, for about a year and is not able to help me. I do not have anywhere to live in my home country except my father's house, and I am afraid for my life if I return. I have not sought help from the authorities in my home country because I am afraid of my father, and I know of friends who went to the authorities but were sent back home and later killed by their partners. I do not think I would be safe if I returned.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a citizen of the United States. I have been using cannabis for medical purposes since the early 1980s, after being diagnosed with adrenal cancer (pheochromocytoma) in 1968. My condition causes severe symptoms such as dangerous spikes in blood pressure, headaches, heart palpitations, and other life-threatening complications. After conventional treatments failed to control my symptoms, I began using cannabis, which has been the most effective way to manage my illness and has allowed me to survive far longer than expected.

For over sixteen years, I was able to use cannabis in my home state without incident. In 1999, following an anonymous tip, law enforcement began investigating me for allegedly growing and selling cannabis. My home was searched, and I was arrested and charged with multiple felony offences, including cultivation and possession of cannabis for sale, as well as possession of other substances. I maintained that my cannabis use and cultivation were strictly for medical purposes, and I was deputized as a medical cannabis agent by the City of Oakland. At my trial, I raised a medical necessity defence, and the jury could not reach a unanimous verdict on the cannabis-related charges, resulting in a mistrial. The prosecution decided not to retry me on those charges, but I was convicted of possession of mescaline and psilocyn, which I asserted were for research purposes.

I was sentenced to 120 days of house arrest, a fine, and three years probation. The court allowed me to use cannabis during my sentence, but the prosecutor appealed, and my conviction for possession of mescaline was reinstated as a felony. I sought to serve my sentence in San Francisco, where attitudes toward medical cannabis are more tolerant, but ultimately, I left the United States for Canada before serving my sentence, while the details of my sentence were still being resolved. My family had already moved to Canada for business reasons. I did not return to the United States to serve my sentence, and a warrant was issued for my arrest. I have not paid my fines or complied with probation.

I fear returning to my home country because I was targeted by law enforcement due to my political activism in support of medical cannabis and my public profile as a former gubernatorial candidate and outspoken advocate. If I am prosecuted or imprisoned, I will be denied access to cannabis, which I need to manage my life-threatening illness. Without cannabis, I am at risk of severe medical complications or death.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am a transgender woman from my home country. From a young age, I experienced discrimination and violence because of my gender identity. I left my home country for the first time in my late teens or early twenties to go to the United States. I returned briefly to care for my dying mother, then went back to the United States, where I lived for several years without legal status. I frequently traveled between the two countries, especially to obtain female hormones. I underwent gender reassignment surgery in my home country. I tried to return and live with my sister, but after a few months, I went back to the United States. I later married an American citizen who wanted to sponsor me, but my application was rejected because of a criminal conviction.

I was advised by a government lawyer to plead guilty, served time in prison, and completed probation.

When living conditions became more difficult in the United States, I returned to my home country. I found that attitudes toward transgender people had not improved. I was prohibited from participating in community activities and faced harassment from police and neighbors. I was denied jobs, including at a telemarketing company, despite meeting all requirements. I was often forced into prostitution to survive, where I was regularly extorted and harassed by police. I tried to file complaints about police abuse, but my concerns were ignored. I also experienced ridicule and discrimination when trying to obtain official documents. Because of my transgender identity, I fear that if I return to my home country, I will continue to face discrimination, violence, and lack of protection from the authorities.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born in Jaffna, but my family moved to live with relatives when I was an infant due to troubles in my hometown. We returned to Jaffna in 2002 after the road was open following the ceasefire. I completed grade 11 in 2006. From 2007 until 2008, I worked as a labourer in my hometown.

Before finishing school in 2006, the army began rounding up students on Saturdays about once a month. I was picked up during these roundups. In 2007, an army patrol questioned me and told me to sign in regularly at the army camp. One day, an army patrol took my identity card, and I had to go to the army camp to retrieve it. When I got it back, I was told I would have to come back every week to sign in. I usually had to sign in twice a week, sometimes three times. Each time, I was asked the same questions about the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and whether I could identify LTTE members. I was also slapped by different people each time. These episodes, occurring regularly for about a year, felt like mental torture to me.

From 2006, there were weekly round-ups where a "head-shaker" would identify LTTE members. On one occasion, ten boys were taken away. Another time, one of my teachers was kidnapped and murdered. After these experiences, I decided I had to leave my home country. I paid 40,000 rupees to a political group for passage to the capital and left Jaffna in 2008. My mother arranged for an agent to get me to Thailand, and I departed my home country in 2008. In Thailand, I registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. In 2009, the agent took me to another country, where I stayed until I was put on a small boat. On September 3, 2009, I boarded the Ocean Lady and arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009, where I claimed refugee protection at the port of entry.

While in the capital, I was arrested one day before leaving for Thailand because I am a Tamil, and was released only because I could show I had a ticket to Thailand. I fear returning to my home country because I would be suspected of links to the LTTE due to my ethnicity, my history of being questioned and detained, and my journey to Canada on the Ocean Lady, which authorities associate with the LTTE.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 24-year-old citizen of my home country. Since 1999, I worked in the international department of a major bank whose majority shareholder was a government entity. In 2001, the bank’s management began collaborating with the new government to investigate corruption and money laundering. I was assigned to compile records of large international transfers since 1990 and was given access to all computerized data. I accepted these duties because I supported the fight against corruption.

After I began this work, I started receiving anonymous phone calls at my office and home. The callers claimed to be from the intelligence service and threatened to kill me if I did not hand over the original documents with compromising information. I also noticed I was being followed. I knew my investigation was implicating many civil servants and military members. I told my superior, who advised me to be careful but encouraged me to continue.

One day in 2001, after I had nearly finished compiling the information, I was intercepted near my house by two individuals who identified themselves as members of the national intelligence service. They beat me and threatened to kill me, demanding the original documents. They searched my vehicle but left when a private security agent arrived.

After this attack, I quickly submitted my report to my superior. The report contained evidence against about 25 individuals and companies, including military, public officials, and business people. I feared reprisals, especially since I had refused to cooperate with those who wanted the evidence destroyed. I took a few weeks off, officially as a holiday, but actually went into hiding at a friend’s house. While in hiding, I decided to flee my country.

In 2001, I traveled to the United States using a visa I had obtained earlier. I stayed legally and later applied to extend my stay. After consulting lawyers who said I could not get protection there, I learned I could seek refuge in Canada. I came to the Canadian border in March 2002 to seek protection. I fear vengeance from the powerful individuals implicated in my report, as they have significant resources and connections throughout the country. My family has reported that strange individuals have been seen near their home. I did not seek protection from the authorities in my country because I do not believe they could protect me from these influential people.
